title: Medical Facts for Pilots Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of aeromedical factors, physiological hazards, and fitness for flight from AIM Chapter 8

questions.question: What is hypoxia?
options: A state of oxygen deficiency in the body
questions.explanation: Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs. The brain is highly sensitive to oxygen reduction.

questions.question: At what cabin altitude does night vision begin to deteriorate?
questions.explanation: Night vision deteriorates at cabin altitudes as low as 5,000 feet due to reduced oxygen. This is why supplemental oxygen is recommended for night flights above 5,000 feet.

questions.question: At what altitude do significant effects of hypoxia typically begin for healthy pilots during daytime?
questions.explanation: Significant effects of altitude hypoxia usually don't occur in healthy pilots below 12,000 feet during daytime. From 12,000-15,000 feet, judgment and coordination become impaired.

questions.question: What are common symptoms of hypoxia?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia symptoms include: headache, drowsiness, dizziness, euphoria OR belligerence, impaired judgment, memory loss, blue fingernails (cyanosis), and tunnel vision.

questions.question: What is hyperventilation?
options: Abnormal increase in breathing rate that reduces CO2
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation is an abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed that blows off excessive CO2. Can be caused by stress, anxiety, or hypoxia itself.

questions.question: How can you treat hyperventilation?
options: Slow your breathing rate and breathe into a paper bag
questions.explanation: Treat hyperventilation by consciously slowing your breathing rate and depth. Breathing into a paper bag helps restore CO2 levels. If using oxygen, first ensure it's working properly.

questions.question: What is unique about the symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia?
options: Their early symptoms are similar and can occur together
questions.explanation: Early symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia are similar (lightheadedness, tingling). They can occur simultaneously. If on oxygen and experiencing symptoms, first ensure oxygen system is working.

questions.question: What causes carbon monoxide poisoning in aircraft?
options: Exhaust fumes entering cabin, often through heater
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide enters the cabin through exhaust fumes, typically via cracks in the heater shroud around the exhaust manifold. CO is colorless and odorless.

questions.question: If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning in flight, what should you do?
options: Turn off heater, open vents, land as soon as practical
Nothing, it will clear on its own
questions.explanation: If CO poisoning is suspected: shut off heater, open air vents, use supplemental oxygen if available, and land as soon as practical. Seek medical attention.

questions.question: What is spatial disorientation?
options: Inability to determine aircraft position/attitude due to sensory conflicts
questions.explanation: Spatial disorientation is the inability to correctly determine position or attitude due to the brain's misinterpretation of sensory signals, particularly when visual references are lost.

questions.question: What is 'the leans'?
options: An illusion where pilot feels banked when actually level
questions.explanation: The leans occur when a gradual bank isn't sensed, then correction creates the illusion of banking the opposite way. Pilot may lean toward the perceived vertical or roll back to original bank.

questions.question: What is the somatogravic illusion?
options: Rapid acceleration creating the illusion of nose-up attitude
questions.explanation: Somatogravic illusion: rapid acceleration (e.g., takeoff) creates false sensation of nose-up pitch. Pilot may push nose down into dangerous attitude. Rapid deceleration creates opposite effect.

questions.question: What causes the 'black hole' approach illusion?
options: Approach over water or unlit terrain on a dark night
questions.explanation: The black hole approach occurs over water or dark featureless terrain at night. Without visual cues, pilots tend to fly lower approaches than intended, risking CFIT.

questions.question: How long does it take for complete dark adaptation?
questions.explanation: Complete dark adaptation requires about 30 minutes in total darkness, though moderate adaptation occurs within 20 minutes under dim red cockpit lighting.

questions.question: What impairs dark adaptation?
options: Bright light exposure, smoking, carbon monoxide, altitude above 5,000 feet
questions.explanation: Dark adaptation is impaired by exposure to bright light (even briefly), smoking, carbon monoxide, cabin altitude above 5,000 feet, and Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.question: How should pilots scan for other traffic?
options: Quick sweeping motion across entire sky
Systematic series of short movements with stops to focus
questions.explanation: Effective scanning requires short, regularly spaced eye movements with stops to focus. The eye detects motion best in peripheral vision but needs to stop to detect stationary targets.

questions.question: What is the IMSAFE checklist used for?
options: Self-assessment of pilot fitness for flight
questions.explanation: IMSAFE: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating (Emotion). A personal checklist for assessing fitness to fly before each flight.

questions.question: How long before flight must a pilot wait after consuming alcohol?
options: 8 hours and must have blood alcohol below 0.04%
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.17: No flying within 8 hours after drinking alcohol OR while under the influence OR with blood alcohol concentration of 0.04% or greater.

questions.question: What effect does alcohol have at altitude?
options: Effects are magnified due to reduced oxygen
questions.explanation: Alcohol's impairing effects are magnified at altitude. Altitude multiplies the effect of alcohol because both reduce oxygen supply to the brain.

questions.question: What is the recommended wait time after scuba diving before flying above 8,000 feet?
questions.explanation: After diving: wait at least 12 hours for non-decompression dives, 24 hours for decompression dives, before flying above 8,000 feet to avoid decompression sickness.

questions.question: What is the primary cause of G-LOC (G-induced Loss of Consciousness)?
options: Blood draining from the brain during positive G maneuvers
questions.explanation: G-LOC occurs during positive G maneuvers when blood is forced from the brain toward the lower body. Symptoms progress from gray-out to tunnel vision to blackout to unconsciousness.

questions.question: What is 'red-out'?
options: Blood pooling in the head during negative G maneuvers
questions.explanation: Red-out occurs during negative G (push-over) maneuvers when blood is forced toward the head. Results in red vision due to blood pressure in the eyes.

questions.question: How does fatigue affect pilot performance?
options: Impairs judgment, slows reactions, reduces attention
questions.explanation: Fatigue impairs judgment, increases reaction time, reduces attention span, affects memory, and leads to poor decisions. Both acute and chronic fatigue are hazardous.

questions.question: What visual illusion can make a runway appear farther away than it is?
questions.explanation: A runway narrower than usual can make it appear farther away, leading to a lower approach. A wider runway creates the opposite illusion. Always use VASI/PAPI when available.

questions.question: What is the most important sense for safe flight?
questions.explanation: Vision is the most important sense for safe flight. In VMC, vision provides orientation. In IMC, pilots must trust instruments over vestibular (balance) Sensations.
